newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Water experts to tackle "challenge of 21st century".
newsitem.headline: Water experts to tackle "challenge of 21st century".

text.p: The world's water resources, over which doomsayers have forecast future conflicts, come under the microscope on Friday at a meeting of experts, decision-makers and officials controlling much finance.

Experts describe water supplies as one of the main challenges of the 21st century, a view echoed by the World Water Council which is organising the gathering in the southern Moroccan city of Marrakesh of scientists, bankers, U.N. and other officials from five continents.

"To preserve water...is a vital and universal priority. To preserve it is to manage it, to take urgent decisions when the lives of thousands of people, indeed entire populations, depend on it..." it said in a statement.
The two-day meeting coinciding with U.N. World Water Day will look at the outlook for world water supplies and ways of managing them. It follows a mixed focus on water in the past two weeks.

Water experts meeting in Muscat warned Gulf Arab states last week that they could face acute water shortages within a century unless serious policies were adopted to rationalise consumption and find cheaper desalination technology.

In Morocco, King Hassan inaugurated a $968 million dam on Thursday whose 3.8 billion cubic metre reservoir capacity will bring the country's irrigated land to one million hectares (2.5 million acres). The project will boost agriculture and provide drinking water and power.

And in a tool that should help water management in years ahead, scientists in Washington said this month they had created an electronic atlas that needed only seconds to show rainfall and climate data for any neighbourhood, region, country or continent.
The head of the Sri Lankan-based International Irrigation Management Institute, David Seckler, said the atlas would become valuable as competition for water became stronger.

In Marrakesh, the experts, including U.N., World Bank, non-government agencies and development banks, will look at the main problems the future holds, including energy, enviroment, health, food security and climatic changes.
"It will conclude with the presentation of a project for a world water charter..." the council said.
UNESCO director-general, Federico Mayor who will open the second day's session, said in a statement that water would be one of the great challenges of the next century.
"It will be necessary to show proof, in action, wisdom and vision, if we want to satisfy humanity's needs and avoid the most precious of natural resources becoming an object of conflict," he said.
